utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to continue with your examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone please be adjusted. Interpreters note, we cannot hear the speaker. The other microphones in the courtroom are on. We can hear other background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said that on the 27th of April, 1999, five Serb policemen were killed and, as he says, the Serb forces attacked the village of Dobros where some villagers were killed. After that, the villagers fled in the direction of Meja. And as he says, the Serb forces stopped the convoy on the road to Meja, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, who said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what Witness Beqe Beqaj said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beqe Beqaj. Yesterday I even gave the transcript pages where he was speaking but then the hearing was adjourned because our time was up yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they separated 24 men who they sent to Hasanaj dolina, and then they singled out 13 of them and the police told them that they were guilty of the killing of Serb policemen and the witness said that no one ever saw these people again. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, or quite simply I have no knowledge of something like that having happened. Had something like that happened, I certainly, as commander of the garrison and commanding officer in Djakovica, would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Nika Peraj testified here. His transcript is rather lengthy. I'm going to put a few questions to you on the basis of his statement, because from his testimony and his statement, it is evident that he was a member of your brigade, that he was one of your subordinate officers. Do you know who Nika Peraj was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nik Peraj was captain first class in the 52nd Brigade, whose commander I was. So he was subordinated to me. Not directly to me but to my Chief of Staff or, rather, in the chain of command he ranked third down the line of subordination. He came in December 1998 from Pristina. That's when he was transferred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He says that he was in the Artillery Rocket Brigade in Djakovica. That is paragraph 4 of his statement. That he was in charge of security of the command of the brigade that was in the Djakovica barracks, and he trained soldiers in the field of security and took care that they did their duties in relation to the security of the command. Was that it briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Djakovica there were two barracks, Metohija and Devet Jugovica. The command of my brigade was in the Metohija barracks and that was his task. This is a task that corresponds to an officer of his rank and his position. That is to say that he got the duty that any officer with that kind of training and rank would have got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Here in tab 4 and 4A you can find documents that pertain to him precisely and what he did. So please look at tab 4. This has to do have -- about the functioning of perimeter security in the Metohija barracks and Captain Peraj Nika is responsible for that. You signed that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's my order. I signed it, and I -- on the 24th of May, 1999, and in this way I regulated his duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other documents in this same tab has to do with the order issued by you to commanders of artillery battalions, and in paragraph 5 it says that on behalf of the command brigade, Captain First Class Nika Peraj will do this.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was his duty. And that is what he dealt with primarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we've established that, your direct relationship with him, the fact he was in your brigade. What does he say in his statement? In paragraph 7, he says that there were paramilitary formations there where the following units were - this is paragraph 7 - Arkan's Tigers, Seselj's White Eagles, and the unit of Franko Simatovic called the Frenkijevci, Frenki's men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right at all. There weren't any paramilitary units in Kosovo and Metohija. The only paramilitary formation in Kosovo and Metohija was the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Further on in paragraph 9 he says MUP and groups from the Territorial Defence launched attacks against civilian targets. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The MUP only carried out anti-terrorist actions, always in a situation when it had been attacked before that or provoked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of his statement he refers to you personally. He says as soon as NATO started bombing, smaller groups started coming in, five to ten people, usually those who were interested in looting, and they joined the army of Yugoslavia. Many of them looked unkempt and were engaged in crime beforehand. They had been recruited from prisons. One night, a group of people came from Russia, one of which was a doctor. They were sent to Kosare after Commander Milos Djosan refused their request to stay in Djakovica saying that he would not allow them to loot. I think that there was a total of 50 such persons. The Territorial Defence of the municipality they came from was paying them, and the Ministry of Defence financed in return the Territorial Defence units. What is correct out of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of this is correct. The only correct thing is that I was commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 11 it says there were Albanians and Roma who were loyal to Serbia. Their commander was Nikola Micunovic, nicknamed Dragan, a major.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please read slower. We don't have the text, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking you to read more slowly. They do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is talking about Micunovic as commander of some unit of the Kosovo Albanians and Roma. Also members of Frenki's unit that I'm going to talk about later. For a while they were reservists under Micunovic's command, and then they joined with Frenki's men. What is true out of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is true. Micunovic was commander of the 13th Military Territorial Detachment from the military department of Pec. He was not my subordinate in any way, but in peacetime one of his depots was in the barracks where I was commander, and there was no other subordination between him and me. And there was no need for him to report to me or could I command him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is any of this correct, that under his command there were some - how should I put this? - some persons who later become Frenki's men?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true absolutely. There were no paramilitaries there, no Frenki's men. Under his command were the personnel of the 113th Military Territorial Detachment. These were primarily Serbs and a few Albanians from the area around Djakovica and Djakovica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, he explains or, rather, presents an alleged fact here in paragraph 13. He says: "One brigade of Republika Srpska that numbered up to 1.000 men arrived on the eve of the NATO bombing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We would be assisted by having this on the overhead projector. It was an existing exhibit in the case; it's in the 92 bis package. I do have one copy here. The accused should really make exhibits available, even if they are formal exhibits, so that the Chamber can follow them in written form. It's up to the Chamber, but if you want to see it on the overhead projector we could probably make ours available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was thinking the same thing. Mr. Milosevic, do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Mr. Robinson. My assumption was that precisely for the reasons mentioned by Mr. Nice because this had been exhibited there was no need to prepare copies of his statement in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Even if it is an existing exhibit, Mr. Milosevic, we still have to find it, and that is your -- that's your duty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, then, that Mr. Nice could be so kind as to provide his copy, because otherwise I won't be able to put questions. This is my very own marked copy and I want to check this out, I want to see what is correct, what is not correct. I assume that it will not present too great a difficulty to Mr. Nice to provide his own copy for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am in the circumstances in possession of the document. I can lay it on the overhead projector. But the accused knows perfectly well that this has got to be dealt with by him. He can rely on me to help whenever I'm in a position to do so, of course, but he really should obey by -- play by the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are grateful to you, Mr. Nice, for letting us have a copy of that. Mr. Milosevic, in future, and I think you know this, you must prepare copies of exhibits for the Court, even if they're already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not even put this on the exhibit list. I'm asking the witness about the testimony of a previous witness who testified about a great many things and who was his subordinate officer. So I'm putting questions to him on the basis of which you should be able to see whether this witness was telling the truth or not, like many other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not the procedure that we follow here, and you very well know that. So, in future, I want you to abide by the procedure and have copies prepared for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. May I continue now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in paragraph 13 he says that a brigade from Republika Srpska had come. He says they were deployed in Rezina, they had insignia on which Republika Srpska was written. Their commander was a lieutenant colonel. First name unknown, last name Vukovic. That brigade arrived in Djakovica in end February, early March, 10 to 20 days before NATO bombing. They had T55 tanks and anti-aircraft artillery which they had probably brought from Republika Srpska. And so on. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. Anyone who knows Djakovica, and he should know Djakovica because he grew up there, Rezina is an area overlooking Djakovica where you cannot hide even a car so as to make it invisible. So there's no shrubbery, no brush, nothing. And to place an armoured brigade in a small area like that is simply impossible. Generally speaking, this man is not qualified. He has not completed a single vocational academy, and it is unreasonable to expect such answers from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell him -- could you tell me, was there any kind of unit from Republika Srpska in Djakovica at all, never mind the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such unit at any time. And I'm sorry that I didn't have time enough to describe the course of my career before the Trial Chamber, because it would clarify this issue as well, and by the leave of the Trial Chamber I would like to do so now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, regarding your career, what can you tell us that is relevant to this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how did does this bear on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the relevance to this issue is none, but he is apologising for not having described his career in full yesterday as he should have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He can send us a note after completing his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence about the other aspects of his career. I wanted to ask you, General, you say that this man is not qualified and it was unreasonable to expect such answers from him. What qualifications did he lack which would have impacted on the kind of evidence that he gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he did not know where armoured units can or cannot be placed. I'm not saying that Nik Peraj did not distinguish between a car and a tank, but anyone with a military education could ever dream of using Rezina, which is visible as on the palm of your hand from Djakovica to hide an armoured brigade. An armoured brigade has 90 tanks, and he mentioned two brigades. So anyone who has the slightest understanding of how and where armoured units are deployed could not say such a thing. Nik Peraj graduated from a teachers' school and became a reserve officer, and that's why he was just a captain at the age of 53, which is very rare in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, all I'm interested in are the facts that he mentioned. I asked you if there had been any unit from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not single unit from Republika Srpska. There were no units from anywhere except the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP, that is the units that were in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, and I won't read it all, not to waste time, he says: "I saw with my own eyes how the members of that brigade from the RS have meetings in Djosan's office."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Djosan, were there volunteers from Republika Srpska who joined the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. In my unit, there was one woman, a volunteer. Her name was Dragojanka, and she was in the 3rd Artillery Battalion under Commander Pasinovic. I wrote about her in my book. She was a nurse, a native Republika Srpska, and she was placed in a unit of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was she the only volunteer from Republika Srpska or were there other volunteers from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was the only volunteer in my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I will skip the part about tanks because I questioned General Delic about it, and he gave quite sufficient explanation. We are not going to waste our time on that. In paragraph 18 he says during the bombing, the military police and part of the staff security of the brigade command were located in a house opposite the barracks in Djakovica, and it was in that house that first discussion was held about carrying out an operation in Meja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. Quite simply, such operations - in fact, they're not operations, they are anti-terrorist actions - are not discussed in houses. All such actions followed regular procedure of planning development in staff headquarters which is the only place for such activities. There were no informal agreements, discussions or informal orders outside premises specifically designated for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 40, I'm going to skip some of them because I don't want to waste too much time on this witness, he says: "In my assessment, there were about 200 paramilitary men in the Djakovica area, most of whom were Arkan's and Seselj's, with about 30 from Frenki's. VJ officers and locals were saying the Frenki's (also known as the Black Hand) were the worst. Members of these groups had rough backgrounds - prison, drug use." And then further on he says where they were quartered, billeted. It says: "Frenki's men were based in a building between the Vllamzini stadium and the gymnasium school on Dimitrije Tucovic Street in Djakovica." He also explains that his former neighbour Bato Dzurdzevic told him about this. He says they stole cars from the citizenry, et cetera. He says: "200 paramilitaries, most of them Arkan's and Seselj's men, 30 or so, Frenki's men." What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat my previous answer. In Djakovica or in all of Kosovo and Metohija, there were no paramilitary units. And when I say "no paramilitary units," that means no Arkan's men, and no Seselj's men, no Frenki's men. This is a product of his imagination. And he must have had some reason for saying this. If that had been true and he had known about it, he had to report it to me as his commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, would it be correct, then, if he said there were -- there had been 200 volunteers from Serbia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite hear the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it be correct for him to say that there had been 200 volunteers in Djakovica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A volunteer is a different notion from the notion of paramilitary units. I had volunteers in my own unit. Those were people who were recruited from the reserve force of the army of Yugoslavia, who responded to the call-up of their own free will, who came to us and were deployed in units of the army of Yugoslavia. I had some volunteers in my units. One of them was killed by terrorists. A volunteer is not a paramilitary. It is a patriot who voluntarily responded to the call-up and joined the army. We placed these people in different units, the volunteers, depending on their training, qualifications, and abilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many volunteers did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my brigade there were 53 volunteers who had been brought from the command of the Pristina Corps by a commander who had brought them together with full accompanying documentation. And depending on what they had done in the army before, they were deployed in various units. Most of those volunteers were later transferred to different units, because anti-aircraft defence units require younger personnel with better eyesight and specific training. Some volunteers were transferred to the 152nd Brigade in the border belt, but they were transferred following regular procedure in the army. So it is improper to confuse the notion of volunteer with the notion of paramilitary. I think it would be a great injustice to those people who served their country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I just ask one further question on the same subject. We've heard evidence of political parties organising the provision of volunteers. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us wrap up this issue that Mr. Kwon brought up regarding volunteers. Apart from the fact that somebody came voluntarily rather than being recruited as part of his military obligation, did the status of such a person differ in any way from any other man in the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such a person had no special status, no privileges. He had the same duties and obligations as anybody else in the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any units made up exclusively of volunteers or would volunteers be scattered across different units depending on their training and qualifications and prior experience?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were placed in one unit or another depending on their wartime assignment, and there were no units made up exclusively of volunteers. There were no units that contained even as much as one-third of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that in a platoon of 30 people it was impossible to have ten volunteers among them.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was not possible. And all the commanders were exclusively active-duty commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 35, among other things, he says: "In Pastrik hotel there was a lot of drinking. So Colonel Djosan, who was the commander in Djakovica tried to put an end to it but was not successful. One time Djosan ordered me to put a stop to this drinking bout, but I did not do that. I did not manage, because the people in the hotel were totally drunk, armed and dangerous."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I had issued an order as garrison commander banning alcohol, and there were violations because soldiers from Kosare occasionally came to phone their families as long as the post office operated. There was a hotel but only non-alcoholic beverages were served there. It's not true that I ever asked this man to go and put a stop to some sort of drinking party, because I would have never done that seeing that he is an Albanian, and I would never have put him in such a position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that: "Paramilitaries could be distinguished from other units by insignia. There was a sign of White Eagles shown to me by investigator Paolo Pastore Stocchi, and I recognised it as the one I had seen in Meja."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no such insignia except insignia of the army, the military police, or the police. Nobody could have worn any other insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when he speaks about command and control in paragraph 36, he says: "All armed groups (VJ, MUP, others) were subordinate to the VJ in theory. The other groups were those such as Seselj's and Frenki's men and the Territorial Defence. The paramilitary ones tended not to be responsive to VJ direction, even though the VJ tried; they followed their own agendas. Their main agenda was a Greater Serbia as intended by the politicians who formed them." What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that this is plain fabrication. Words are used that have been thought up by other minds. There were no paramilitaries. Army units were subordinated to army commanders. Police units were subordinated to police commanders. There were no paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "The following people attended meetings that were held daily at 800 hours and 1800 hours every day. Momcilo Stanojevic, Meja, Micunovic, head of the military department, Camovic head of DB in Djakovica, Miodrag Adamovic, head of MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph down Mr. Nort. Paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is an enumeration of the people who attend, and I just reached your name when Mr. Nice intervened. "Milos Djosan, commander of Pristina Corps, and Lazarevic, Jeftovic, Kotur occasionally."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. My command, the command of the 52nd Brigade, was located in the Metohija barracks which is the barracks that were not targeted at all and where the Italian contingent of KFOR set up later on. In my barracks we had reporting and briefing that was attended by my subordinates, my subordinate officers, the command, and you can see that from all my regular combat reports and the briefing sessions. In the Devet Jugovica barracks, which was located in quite a different part of town where there was a forward command post, meetings were attended by the commander or, rather, the Chief of Staff usually at the corps and someone from the corps command and I myself as the brigade commander who was there, and if the need arose, officers from certain arms and services of the command of the Pristina Corps. There were no meetings which were attended, especially not regular meetings attended by Camovic. I never saw Camovic at any of these meetings. He would come from -- or, rather, the president of the Djakovica municipality would come from time to time but just when matters relating to the garrison were discussed because I was the garrison commander as well. So that certain questions relating to the garrison and its activities I did cooperate with the president of the municipality and the head of MUP of Djakovica, but nobody else attended the briefings, because briefings are separate meetings and rules govern who can attend and nobody can attend unless there are orders from his superior. Even officers, high-ranking officers, cannot be present unless they are ordered to do so by a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But now he goes on to speak at those meetings, and he says in paragraph 40: "Once I had to separate Djosan from Micunovic after a meeting because they were arguing. I do not know what they were arguing over." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So he says he separated you from Micunovic not to come to blows, to stop fighting and arguing. "And on the same occasion. Once Djosan got into the car with me," he goes on to say, "he said that Kovacevic and Micunovic were doing unauthorised things and blaming it on the army. Micunovic's unit from the reserve force at the end of March killed eight civilians in the village of Deva." That's what he says. He says that this was confirmed by Peko Djurdjevic because he was in that same unit.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a complete fabrication. Can you imagine me being in a situation as commander of the garrison fighting an officer who is not even my subordinate or arguing with him? That's absolutely impossible. It would be a violation of military regulations. Had I wanted to do so there would be other ways of dealing with the matter, arresting him for example. But none of this is true. I was never in a car with Nik Peraj. I had my own driver and I had three cars. I used three different cars depending on where I was doing. Why would the captain need me to drive me when I had my own driver soldier who was there to drive me where I wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what do you know about this assertion of his, what he says here that the soldiers from that reserve unit of Micunovic's at the end of March killed eight civilians in the village of Deva?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I never heard about that. At the briefing session that we had at the forward command post of the corps, I would have to have known that because Micunovic's detachment or unit was subordinated to the forward command post of the Pristina Corps as is provided for by the security schedule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll skip over a few paragraphs. He says in paragraph 41 that you called him from a meeting and said that the unit that was near Ljug Bunar should be moved to Kosare. "I then had to pass this information on to the ARBR operation staff, Major Zdravko Vinter. This unit was part of Djosan's brigade."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was referring to my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know the system of command. If I wanted to move a unit, then I would order the commander of the unit to undertake the movement of the unit. That is the system of command and control. I would issue orders to the commanders of the artillery battalions and then the artillery battalions would go down the line and issue orders further down to the subordinate officers. So I couldn't have sent him as a courier to convey my orders. That would be impossible. That is just pure fabrication and doesn't correspond to the truth of the matter at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 45, next please, it says the following: "During the Meja incident, the MUP set up check-points." Was there an incident in Meja at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any Meja incident, no. There was an anti-terrorist operation in Meja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Anyway, the MUP set up check-points because it was a better position to check identification cards and decided who should be allowed to pass by freely. At the check-points, the MUP took away ID cards and money from people. I believe that the MUP probably already had the intention of meting out revenge for the killing of Prascevic and four other officers, knew which area they wanted to target for revenge and asked the VJ to assist using the reason that they needed the VJ to provide security against the KLA or UCK attacks. He says: "I do not believe that there were any UCK/KLA units in the area at that time." What did you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is common knowledge that part of -- that it belongs to the general area called Reka and there were many terrorists and I spoke about that yesterday. It is an area where terrorists are engaged in large-scale operations and activities, and it is true that the terrorists killed five policemen. He mentions Prascevic. I knew Prascevic myself. He wasn't the chief of MUP but I did know him. But as for Meja, it was an anti-terrorist operation exclusively which was legal, lawful, with the aim of rounding up the killers of those policemen. Otherwise, at that time we had a lot of losses and casualties, particularly policemen but civilians as well who were loyal to us. Not too many in that region, Albanians who were loyal to the authorities and to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have on the overhead projector this next map now, please. [In English] Would you be so kind as please to put to the ELMO. [Interpretation] Now, what does that map show us, General? I have just pulled it out of this binder. I cannot find the exhibit number, but I will do so, and I'll be able to tell you in due course to see which tab it's come out of.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map we can see how the anti-terrorist operation in Meja unfolded. We see part -- the part that relates to my unit, the 2nd Motorised Battalion. My brigade -- or part of my brigade, rather, took part in that operation with the aim of effecting --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, part of my unit, one infantry company, that was its strength, took part here. There were platoons here from the rear battalion. And I said yesterday that all my combat units were outside Djakovica, and I gave you the places where they were deployed. In Djakovica was the logistics rear battalion and the command artillery battalion, both of which are not combat units, and they had the assignment in -- along this axis from trig 478 to elevation or feature 442, provide security and ensure that the terrorist forces from this area here which is marked on the map and is called Reka, it is a forest area where there were a lot of terrorists, to prevent them from flowing into this area and coming into the town of Djakovica and jeopardising our units there, and this is where our units were located. One of my positions was here. Then there was a command post for the 3rd Artillery Battalion in the Beqe region here and also a command in the town of Djakovica proper. My right-wing neighbour was the 2nd Motorised Battalion from the 549th Brigade, and you can see that in this area here and there. And its commander was Colonel Vukovic. Colonel Vukovic, yes. The 113th Military Sector, which Nik Peraj mentions, whose commander was Micunovic, was located in this area here, quite a long way away. Far away from me and from Vukovic as well. My units had the exclusive task of preventing this overflow, and I personally toured the unit that was commanded by Major Odak, and I came across them at the position they were supposed to be deployed at. Now, in view of the fact that the terrorists had not or were not in this area here and were not moving towards the positions held by our units, our units didn't come into contact at all with members of the Siptar forces. My soldiers and officers didn't even see a single terrorist. And you can see that on the basis of the report that was written where not a single bullet was fired, was used. They spent two days there. They spent the night there. And on this map we can see that they didn't move positions at all. If a unit moves its position, then this is displayed in a different way. For example, this unit here moved its positions. From this position, from this area it moved to take up its positions to the north. The unit that was from within my own composition, that is the Logistics Battalion, one of its companies under the command of Major Odak was located in that area, and that is the -- what relates to Meja and refers to my unit, and that is what I'm aware of. On the other hand, we know that that was the period of the fiercest bombing, the heaviest bombing, the border belt around the frontier, and we as a unit had many more important tasks to attend to than this one here. So this area, the Reka area, was supposed to be an operative base for the landing. What Normandy was for the Allies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, who compiled this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I compiled this map together with Major Odak, who was the commander of that particular unit after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After being called by the commission which was established, which was set up to investigate the alleged events in Meja on the basis of the book that came out published by the democratic forum. So that map was compiled at that time on the basis of statements by subordinate officers and on the basis of knowledge and documentation and information that we have dating back to that time contemporaneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there actually a date on it showing us when it was compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there is no date. But I can tell you that it was compiled when the statement was written, a day or two after the writing of the statement. And I think that you will find a date on the statement, when it was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us make one point more precise with respect to the question I asked you. Nika Peraj says that he didn't believe that at that time in the area there was a single unit of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course that is pure fabrication and the greatest lie that could have been uttered. Who else would we have engaged against then? The forces of Yugoslavia engaged against whom? The civilian population was never a target either of the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the KLA forces, what strength were they in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three KLA brigades were in the area at the time. This was very suitable ground, lots of forest, wooded area, and they could take in forces from Kosare. And it was -- an operation was imminent, and in fact they did have some success at the initial stage to break through, but this was the best and shortest way if they managed to pass Kosare to stop them in that area there. And the command, the corps command, sizing the situation understood what it would mean if the forces were to join up, the Kosare forces of the terrorists were to join up. And there were three brigades of them. They had support from Albania, the artillery from Albania, and they had fire support from NATO -- the NATO's air force. And you know what terrorists and aviation joins up, when an air force and terrorists join up you know what can be expected, what happens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. Let's move on. Paragraph 46 of his statement. Paragraph 46 he mentions in -- paragraph 46 of the statement he says: "The commander of the military security was Momir Stojanovic and he was a good friend of mine. At the beginning of March 1999, Stojanovic told me about the plan for ethnic cleansing which the Serb forces would implement against the Kosovo Albanians in Djakovica municipality." Well, I've read out the whole paragraph 46. Tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Stojanovic was the head of military security in the Pristina Corps, and he originated -- he was a native from the area of Djakovica. We also know that Nik Peraj throughout the time was a collaborator of the state security service or, rather, the military security service, and on that basis, on those grounds, he was sent to Djakovica, Nik Peraj was. And I cannot but say that -- I cannot say that he didn't help the unit in many matters, Nik Peraj, especially in the period after the breakdown of the anti-terrorist operation at the end of September where there were still weapons and weapons hadn't been returned. So quite probably he did quite a bit for the security service and cooperated with them, collaborated with them. And he was deserving in that area. But knowing Colonel Stojanovic and indeed all our officers, I do not believe that somebody could have had any monstrous idea of that kind, thought up a monstrous idea like that, especially not somebody belonging to an ethnic group that was supposed to be annihilated, destroyed. That would be quite illogical. Had he mentioned somebody else, then perhaps one could have given some thought to the matter. But to tell an Albanian that all the Albanians would be wiped out, and he was himself an Albanian, that seems to me to be quite impossible and beyond belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, many things that defy belief can be heard here, but let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the map is on the ELMO, the general mentioned statements in relation to this map, and I note that this map is tab 20.1, and tab 29 is his statement. So if you could lay some foundation about the statement and let us know what this statement is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you exactly what I stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It is for the accused to lead the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 29, you have a statement to the expert team, to the commission for the cooperation with the ICTY. The date is the 27th of December, 2002. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the unit did on the 28th of April, nineteen-ninety -- is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th and 28th have been dealt with separately because the commission asked us to look at each day in particular, to describe the activities of our units, although from the map you can see that my unit did not move. I had to write a statement nevertheless so that everything would be very precise so that it could be established whether I was telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us just have a look at tab 28 now. It contains the statement that deals with the 27th, and the next one has to do with the 28th. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear again what this expert team is, how they composed of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear you. They did not compile anything. I did. I made this statement to the expert team, and the expert team was established on the basis of the fact that some things appeared including in book about alleged crimes in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In view of the negative experience with Markale and other such deceptions, the expert team was tasked with dealing with this as soon as possible in order to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We heard that yesterday. Mr. Milosevic, is this the same group which General Delic called the VJ commission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is called the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. I assume it's the same. I don't know anything about this commission, so I cannot inform you about that. But it is entitled to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY, and underneath it says "to the expert team." So obviously it's the expert team of the commission. Obviously a commission for cooperation with you here was established, and then they established their own expert team. If the transcript reflects what the general said at the end of his statement in response to your question -- oh, yes, to does say it. It does. It is in the transcript what the general said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he sent it to the commission for cooperation, to the expert team.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't see the English translation here. I assume it is there. Yes, that's what it says, to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. You can see it in the translation too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at what you said here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I -- may I say, speaking at least for myself, I do not see any need to go over with the General statements that he himself has made. These simply need to be adopted by him as accurate accounts of what happened, and he's already, of course, dealt with the matter without reference to the statements. I'm simply expressing my own personal view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite all right, Mr. Bonomy. I'm not going to go through all of this. I just wanted to quote a single sentence in the middle of the first paragraph of your statement related to the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the terrorists, in addition to constant attacks against the SUP and MUP, they carry out total repression over the Siptar population in order to persecute them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not find the exact reference. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not go through the statement, tab 29.1, as Mr. Kwon said a few moments ago. Please, could you look at paragraph 49 of Nika Peraj's statement now. I'm going to skip the explanation. "I was at the meeting when the massacre in Meja was planned because this was going on at the same -- in the same building where I was with my security unit."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that. I haven't got that report, but I can tell you that it's not true at all. I don't know which building it is, and I don't know what kind of planned massacre that is. It is quite incredible that now all of a sudden he says that something happened and that he was not present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, no, he says he was present. And he says: "I was at the meeting when the massacre in Meja was planned."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite incredible, quite incredible that somebody would call him to attend a meeting about a massacre of his own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did anybody have that kind of meeting regardless of inviting Nika Peraj or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I've already said that, and I believe there's no need for me to repeat this. But it is quite certain that not in a single case was any kind of agreement sought on a massacre or any kind of persecution of the civilian population. After all, they were citizens of our country, and what normal, sensible country would do that to its own people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Now, this is a very important part that he testified about here in particular, but I'm not going to dwell on the transcript. The statement will do. It is paragraph 50 of his statement. He says: "On the 28th of April, 1999, the day after Meja and Korenica massacre were committed, I was in the brigade headquarters at the cultural centre in Djakovica. Major Zdravko Vinter," that is subordinate officer of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, assistant commander for information of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. "Who was employed in the personnel office, was preparing a report for the 3rd Army headquarters in Nis. In the report of the VJ, it was stated that 74 terrorists had been killed in Korenica and 68 in Meja. On this occasion, I was able to read over Major Vinter's shoulder part of the -- Vinter used big letters when he typed the report. Vinter used large fonts when typing." Again, he is qualifying it as the massacre in Meja. He is writing a report, and over his shoulder he saw the post-operation report saying terrorists had been killed, 74 in -- 68 in Meja and 74 in Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, there was no massacre in Meja. Secondly, it is not possible that my subordinate officer, a major who could write only to me and report only to me, that he would write to the commander of the 3rd Army. That is a third level in relation to me and fourth in relation to him. So even theoretically it was impossible for him to write that. On the other hand, he did not take part in this, and our unit did not take part in this, and it was not in charge, and there was no need for it to report to anyone about that. So this is totally unrealistic. This corroborates what I said a few moments ago, that Nik Peraj did not have basic military skills. Not a single officer could assume that an official report should be written four rungs above him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be I've missed the evidence on this, but can you remind me, do you say that there were terrorists killed at Meja and at Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. Then you didn't hear me right. I did not say that terrorists were killed in Meja and Korenica. I was just saying where my unit took part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you did. I'm trying to be clear about it. Do you -- I'm asking you now. Do you say that terrorists were killed at Meja or Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in Meja and Korenica there were terrorists and that an anti-terrorist operation was carried out. I said that the members of my unit had no contact, and they never even saw the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you able to tell us whether, nevertheless, any terrorists were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're asking me to say something that I had not seen, and I swore here that I would tell the truth and nothing but the truth. I don't have any knowledge about that, and it was not my duty to report on that. Had my soldiers killed a terrorist, then I would have had to include that in my report to my superior officer. Everything else goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that. Are you saying that no one gave any report to you about whether or not terrorists were killed in either of these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No one informed me about that because I was garrison commander. However, garrisons are not in charge of operations. Garrisons, as units, do not engage in combat activity. They are military territorial organs primarily in charge of securing a particular order, organising supplies for the population, et cetera, but they do not carry out activities and are not in charge of activities as such. I think that I never said anything like that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't suggest you do. I'm asking you these questions because yesterday on a number of occasions you said that if something had happened you were bound to have heard about it. Now, does this not fall into this category? This is not one of those things that if it happened you were bound to have heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I would have heard of that had it happened, but I said that I hadn't heard about it and, therefore, I cannot speak about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that as far as you're concerned no terrorists were killed in either of these locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that I am not aware of anybody being killed. That is not to say that that was not the case altogether. Many things happen without me knowing about it. Perhaps at this very instant somebody is being killed in New York and Washington and I don't know about it. Perhaps this is not a very fortunate example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may not -- I'm not going to simply depart from this in light of the attitude you're adopting to these questions. Are you saying that the events that we're discussing at the moment were not within your area of your responsibility, because you give the example of New York, which is clearly isn't within your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. New York certainly is not, but I said that the air defence units do not have responsibility on the ground. I was responsible for all of Kosovo and Metohija in terms of the air defence, whereas this was part of the area of responsibility of the 125th Brigade and the 549th Brigade. I as brigade commander of the PVO did not have any responsibility over events on the ground nor can I engage in planning or can I carry out any operations except those when I myself am attacked, when my units are attacked. So it is purely defensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you accept that yesterday you said on a number of occasions that when incidents were being put to you, described by other witnesses or in other material, you said, "That could not have happened, because if it had, I would have heard about it." Now, do you accept that you said that on a number occasions? Just answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that about the town of Djakovica, about concrete events that are mentioned in a concrete sense. You asked me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me how this matter that we're exploring at the moment differs from the sort of material that you were able to tell us yesterday you would have known about it if it had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that had I known, I would have reported to my superior officer about this, just like any officer of mine was duty-bound to report to me about that. Since I did not take part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You plainly don't understand my question or you're deliberately avoiding answering it. My question is simply this: Tell me how the present incident differs from the incidents that you said you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bound to have known about in Djakovica. Is it because this falls somehow or other outwith responsibility in a different way or outwith an area you'd be familiar with or what? What is it that's different about this incident, or these two incidents, that make them such that you cannot tell us one way or the other whether people were killed in them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that had an anti-terrorist operation been carried out, that's what I said -- it does happen that people get killed in anti-terrorist actions, but in this concrete case that you are obviously alluding to, I cannot say anything about it because nobody provided any information about Meja, and what you are obviously trying to say to me, and that is that I have not made a statement about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can take this no further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, can I ask you the extent of the contacts that you had with Nik Peraj when he -- when he served with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nik Peraj came to see me about 10 or 15 times, since he was three levels below me in terms of subordination. Before me he would go to report to his Chief of Staff to inform him. Very often he socialised with the head of the security organ, and I already said that he worked for security. As for me, he saw me about ten times, and every time when he reported to me on an ordered assignment, and that was the barracks guards. This was done every seven days, and then he reported to me about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell me generally what impression did you form of his character at that time, of his honesty, his trustworthiness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My impression was that he was an honest man who could be trusted, and that then he would have told me. He would have reported to me had he known about the event at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why would you now then doubt the evidence that he gave during the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very clear what's going on. Maybe I would be saying the same thing now if I were living in Djakovica. General Delic tried to explain this to you. It's very clear what a person has to say if they're in his situation. He most probably gave all or part of his statement under duress, because at the time there was an exist -- there was in existence an order of mine making it obligatory for every commanding officer and every soldier to report any crime they were aware of, and they were free to come and inform me personally. If he had known something at the time and didn't tell me, either he was dishonest then or he was dishonest when he gave the statement. If he had kept mum about it then, then he was guilty of cover-up, or he gave his recent statement under duress. Maybe he is being threatened. He is a man who has three children. I cannot completely understand, but I can only guess at what his situation could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear about one thing more. General Djosan, what you said is this, that you should have known what happened in Djakovica because your subordinates should have told you. But I'm looking at this map. Given that Meja is just the adjacent village to Djakovica, and as for the anti-terrorist operation which took place in Meja, I don't understand why you didn't hear anything about the result of the operation. You should have received a report in one kind or any other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that my subordinate would have reported to me. None of those people in Meja were my subordinates. The 2nd Battalion was not subordinated to me. My subordinated unit that took part in that operation was one company of a Logistics Battalion commanded by certain Vlatko. I hope he will testify here. I went to inspect, but from the place where this unit was deployed, Meja could not even be seen. Meja was at a slight elevation with the forest in front of it, so it was not visible from where I was. The commander of the 2nd Battalion had no duty to report to me. The system of command is such that reports are only sent to your own superiors. I cannot speculate on matters which were not reported to me by my subordinates and of which I have no direct knowledge. All I know is that there had been a anti-terrorist action because my own soldiers, some of them, were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So by the time when you prepared this map, tab 29 in the commission, you should have heard something then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then do you know now how many terrorists were killed in that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you how I heard about it. I actually read about it from a book, a book published by Natasa Kandic. That's the first information I got about events in Meja, and it was on the basis of that that I was invited by the commission and on the basis of that that we wrote our reports. The first knowledge I ever gained about Meja was from that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The number of killed people, be it KLA or civilians, is it correct? The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I don't know whether it happened, I can't say anything about the numbers. I just answer to you that I don't know if anybody was killed, and you go on to ask me if the number is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can -- that's the farthest we can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you saying there is no alternative version of these events which has been established by the commission that you're aware of? Alternative to the book that you're describing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't believe any alternative versions. I cannot tell you simply anything about a matter I completely ignore. The first I ever heard anything about it was from that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but that's a book that the commission was set up to investigate and perhaps either discredit or confirm. Now, as the result of that exercise, has it been confirmed that a number of people who may have been terrorists were killed or has it not been confirmed? Surely you know that through working along with the commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That commission was abolished just after it started its work. When the new minister of defence took over, he immediately stopped that commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me of the identity of the person who worked along with you in compiling the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the commander of this unit, my subordinate officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Commander of which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel Vlatko Odak. He was then commander of a company in my brigade that participated. And I just showed you in which location that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he never -- he never discovered the outcome, whether anyone was killed in the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, come on. Come on, General. Surely in the discussions you had you would at least explore the question whether he was aware of the death of terrorists in that operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked him to write a report describing the condition and the position of our unit. That's all I asked of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying it's not even of any interest to you whether people were killed at that incident or not. You're not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am interested now that so much is being said about it. Now that I have read about it, I would be happy to find out the truth. I'm not saying that the event as such is of no interest to me. It is. It happened in our country, in Kosovo and Metohija, but I'm not able to provide answers about something that I have no direct knowledge of, and I will be happy if the truth is learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's one thing that is not quite clear to me regarding the questions that have been asked of you. You said that an anti-terrorist action had taken place in that area. It involved one of your units.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The task of that unit of yours was the line of blockade you showed on the map. You said that this unit of yours did not carry out any combat activities because it did not run into any of the three KLA brigades that had been present there. You even said they didn't fire a single round because they were not involved in any combat, and the commanders of those units reported to you that they had no combat action and did not fire a single round. Is this why you are not able to provide any explanation as to things that don't refer to your units?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness does not have a microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely the reason. I cannot provide information on matters on which I have no clear and precise knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. Then we will cover another few points regarding this. Let me clarify one more matter. Mr. Bonomy asked you that how come yesterday you said a couple of times, and you indeed said so regarding crimes in Djakovica, that you would have known about them had they happened? What is the job of the garrison commander in Djakovica? There was discussion of several crimes in Djakovica, Milos Gilic Street, Qerim neighbourhood. What is the job of the garrison commander in Djakovica? Is his job to be familiar with the situation in all of the town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison commander is responsible primarily in peacetime but also in war to get informed about events in town. He can get such information from the municipal MUP organs but also from other civil authorities. And he is also responsible for ensuring normal operation, normal life in town as far as possible. But I was, in fact, commander of an air defence brigade. My responsibility, my primary responsibility, was airspace and my own units. As far as the functioning of authorities in Djakovica is concerned, I appointed Major Vinter, one of my subordinates, to attend from time to time meetings within the garrison to regulate problems, any problems that may occur involving civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was within the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 52 in his statement, Nika Peraj says --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... paragraph 52, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will skip the greatest part of this paragraph and read only what refers to you directly. It says: "Djosan did not agree, did not approve of the operation in Korenica and Meja and arrested Micunovic for involvement. Micunovic, however, remained in prison for only three days. I learnt about the arrest of Micunovic from his brother, Aco Micunovic, who was a sergeant in the VJ in Djakovica. Micunovic was released upon personal intervention (I don't know at which level, perhaps political) of Vojislav Seselj and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Sergej Perovic told me this." So it says here that you arrested Micunovic for his reported involvement in what you call an anti-terrorist operation. Did you really arrest him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't even try, because I had no information or reason to have him arrested. If there had been the slightest reason or suspicion, I would have. But what it says here is completely illogical. It says he was arrested and then released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. It says: "Djosan did not approve of the operation in Korenica and Meja and therefore arrested Micunovic for his involvement."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my responsibilities, it was not up to me to approve or not approve of anti-terrorist operation. My primary responsibility were operations in the airspace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't arrest Micunovic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist me with one thing? Was he held in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not that I know of. He was replaced. That's what I know. He was replaced from his position of commander of the 113th Battalion -- Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that immediately following upon the anti-terrorist operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date because he was not subordinated to me, but later, in the course of my inquiries and when I checked, I know that he was replaced in that period because he was not very good at performing his duty of holding the line of blockade that was his task, and you can see that on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was he held in prison for a few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any information about that. I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, Nik Peraj says the following: "Individual witnesses said that the Serbs sprayed gas over the victims to knock them out before they killed them." He says: "I never saw gas canisters in there to confirm this allegation, but I'm convinced that the Serbs used them."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that speaks of his knowledge of the situation and his statement why would anybody sprinkle gas on anyone in an open space to incapacitate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know anything about any gas being used?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never heard anything like that. This is the first piece of information where any sort of gas is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 71, he says that he heard of an incident which took place at the end of March in Djakovica at the address Ymer Grezda Street 134a, I mentioned this yesterday, although my knowledge of the incident is not first-hand knowledge. I did hear that a paramilitary group was responsible for that named the Black Hand which was led by Rajko Pantovic. Now, my question to you is this: Was there ever any paramilitary group called the Black Hand and do you know -- does the name Rajko Pantovic ring a well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Rajko Pantovic is not a name I was familiar with nor do I know -- and actually, I do know that there was never any paramilitary group in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 77, he says: "The MUP had no tanks but had armoured personnel carriers given to them by the army and painted blue. The BOV is something that the VJ and the MUP had. The MUP did not have any Pragas because they didn't know how to use them. The unit of Colonel Djosan had combat armoured vehicles and about 30 Pragas." He says that about your unit or, rather, his own unit because he was in your unit.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. My unit did indeed have Pragas, BOVs or combat armoured vehicles, and the other thing he mentioned. Those were the weapons that they had, and the task was to shoot at targets in the air using those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are all anti-aircraft weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Xhevahire Syla, a witness here, a lady, said that on the 14th of April, 1999, mixed Serb forces entered Nivokaz, Djakovica municipality, stormed Albanian houses, gave the inhabitants five minutes to leave, a convoy towards Djakovica was formed, the police attacked some people in the convoy and told them to go to Albania and said that refugees were not allowed to leave the route to Prizren which was a roundabout way to the border. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. No knowledge about that, and I don't believe that it's true either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear? How are you in a position to say that? How is this incident -- how is this different from the position in relation to the anti-terrorist operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you followed carefully, what it says here is that members of the army of Yugoslavia entered and that it was a lady, a lady witness, and that one of the members of the army of Yugoslavia, or the MUP, entered the house and ordered the people inside to leave. I did not say that there were no anti-terrorist actions, operation; but I do know the army and the police very well, and I can state from when I saw on the spot and what I knew of them that they never did anything against the civilian population. So I assume that your witness was indeed a civilian, was she not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this -- so you base this on your own view of the integrity of the army and the police and on nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base that on my knowledge and familiarity with my unit and the army that I was a member of and the police force that I cooperated with over there constantly, and I know that things like that did not happen. That's what I base that on. I was down there, and I know the people there, the people I worked with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again I'm not sure whether the accused is quoting from oral testimony or from the exhibit. If it's the exhibit, it's Exhibit 270 or 270A, the redacted version of the statement, but again he should have made the statement available to the Court and for us to follow if he's going to quote from it, especially if he's going to quote from it at that speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. You didn't give me instructions of that kind up until now. I will do my best to prepare it for you, but I did quote, Mr. Robinson, on many occasions from witness statements, and there were no requests to place those statements on the overhead projector or to hand them round. And I have been quoting from statements for at least 100 times now. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She goes on to say that the convoy was stopped at a place near the bridge of Bistrazin and that the Serb forces separated people -- or rather, the Serb forces separated from the convoy and then the convoy was hit by NATO strikes, and then three low-flying planes with Serb flags passed over their heads and bombed the convoy seven times and killed 70 to 80 people. So we're talking about Bistrazin or Bistrazin, the bridge there. Do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the statement by this witness is ludicrous. In Bistrazin, on the other hand, I had my unit there. It was a unit which was in charge of securing the Bezim bridge, which is to be found in Bistrazin and is part of the command artillery battalion, and all it did was to mask the bridge, camouflage it. The event that is mentioned, my people were not present during the event and didn't personally see the air force attack on that place near Bistrazin. Now, the fact -- to say that the members of the army accompanied civilians, there's no question of that. And it is even more ludicrous when she goes on to say that she saw this, she was in the column, and that she counted the number of airstrikes by the Serb air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question. Were our planes airborne at all, flying at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had obviously saw NATO planes because our planes were not able to take off five days into the war. What courage and bravery would it take and what kind of NATO forces would they have been had our air force been able to reach Djakovica and then go in to launch seven airstrikes which is what this witness said. And that she was in the column, that she saw insignia or flags or whatever she said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to hear as to what people might or might not have seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed. On the earlier point that you make that the column was not accompanied by Serb soldiers or VJ soldiers, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know is that the army at that time of the fiercest part of the NATO aggression had very important assignments to defend the country from NATO planes, and NATO planes struck the columns as well.
