There were strikes on the columns. So which commander would have sent his own soldiers to accompany a column which might have been the target and indeed was the target of NATO strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, for my own part I see little -- in fact, I don't see any benefit in seeking the logical analysis of a situation by this witness from the point of view of his general views about the integrity of the army and the police. I think we need to hear evidence of his knowledge of circumstances, and I found a lot of the recent evidence pretty pointless for that reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain the sense of all this straight away, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in view of your position as commander of the anti-air defence on the territory, did you, ex officio, have to be informed if any of our planes were flying, were airborne?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I must have been informed. Somebody must have informed me so as to prevent our plane from being shot down by our own forces. So had any of the planes taken off, I would have had to know first, and I had no information of any kind like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My comment, if you were listening to it, did not apply to the evidence about the three planes, and I do see that as a relevant comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've now got the witness's statements if the accused is going to continue asking questions and if they're based on the witness's statements and he let's me know what paragraph of which of the two statements it is, I'll make them available for the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You heard, Mr. Milosevic. What paragraphs are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any more questions with regard to those statements, so I have to save time. I'm not going to continue along that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just some concrete events dating back to March 1999, and I have in mind certain documents that you yourself brought in. Among your documents there was your war diary. Can we now have a look at the most characteristic events of March 1999 that you made a note of in your war diary, entries about that. And it's in tab 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For good order, we've been going through one or two tabs that haven't been exhibited. May I repeat my position in relation to all VJ commission documents and invite the Chamber not to produce them at this stage and await the conclusion of questioning of this witness. I think that in the past, while this same topic's been dealt with, the Chamber has taken the view that statements of the witness himself made on an earlier occasion, whatever the ruling might be about the admissibility of VJ commission produced documents generally, is that they are admitted. If that is -- if I'm right in recalling that as the Chamber as practice, then I dare say that tab 28 and tab 29 might fall into a different category from maps and so on that have been produced for the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may not matter that it was a VJ commission, Mr. Nice, where in relation to this particular map the witness said he was one of the two people who compiled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. That may form a different -- that may form a similar basis for admissibility under the practice of the Court to the statements themselves. Yes, I can see that. But in any event, to avoid the problems that we've been having about exhibits, it might be prudent to get these dealt with straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in tidying up the exhibits, we'll admit tabs 4 and 4.1, tabs 29 and 29.1, and tab 28. The proper reference is to tabs 4 and 4A. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you please bear in mind that we need brief answers and tell us briefly about the contents and entries of your war diary, not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to lose time. We have the first day of the war here, and then several days later you look at several days, several entries for purposes of illustration to see what your war diary was like and what it contains. Just in the briefest terms.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the first day of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You have the first day, sixth day, seventh day, eighth day and so on and so forth. So you have extracted several days. But I don't think we need go through every day, each of these days. Just tell us the basics and then we can move on. We have provided the war diary in the original and of course in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just on that last observation. No doubt the full document is here, and if it could be made available to me now, then I will be able to review the whole document as opposed to the extract overnight. Perhaps it's with the witness; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is the document here, the document in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd have to ask my -- or, rather, the witness that. I don't believe that we have the entire document here, just a few excerpts. I didn't assume that you would be interested in the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, what do you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have parts of my diary, individual days from individual periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you not have the whole diary with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was in agreement with the legal advisors of Mr. Milosevic. I could, of course, have brought in the whole diary from the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't have it in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not. Had I had it in the hotel, you would have had it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will have course be immediately alerted in light of the earlier issues you've raised to what can be seen on the English between pages 2 and 3 is missing entries. We can only do what we can with the material available. Just look at the sequence of dates and remember the questions we're asking, or, rather, the Court was asking. It seems very unfortunate indeed that where from previous witness it was cross-examination of previous witnesses it was known that war diaries are one of the fundamentally important documents that the Prosecution wishes to see they should have brought in a sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a document that's been the subject of a request at any stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that when we were asked to refine down our requests on the grounds that the number of requests we made was too broad, this was one that was then cut off the list or that was not particularised. I'll check that further, but I think that's the position. We had to make a selection, and this is not one of those we in the event selected. But nevertheless, it's clear from all our previous cross-examination, and indeed from the requests we've made, that these documents, where witnesses who are able to produce them turn up, are vitally valuable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, did the war diary remain with the army after your retirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] War diaries are sent to the archives, like all other documents from a certain period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how did you manage to get it to get these extracts from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the advisors of Mr. Milosevic. Zdenko Tomanovic, attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he simply select the parts that he wanted to you bring along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We selected them together. He said, "Select a few," and I thought that the first day was very important, like in any war, this one included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be clear. Mr. Tomanovic sent an official letter to the archives requesting the witness's war diary so that it could be presented here, and indeed he got it and made a selection with the witness so that you would see what this is like. If you require the war diary in its entirety, I'm going to ask Mr. Tomanovic to obtain it the same way, formally, the entire diary of Mr. Djosan -- or, rather, the command of the 52nd Brigade of the air defence. That was published on front page that is here in the photocopy. So then a few examples were taken. But if Mr. Nice needs it in its entirety, we would be very glad to be of assistance so that he can read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in the circumstances, yes, I think the proceedings might be facilitated and helped if you could get the war diary in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll take it upon myself this obligation to have the entire war diary be made available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, since we took this as a subject which is supposed to show what a war diary is all about and since your unit is a very special one being air defence, but who is it that keeps a war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations duty officers at the staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are the entries made according to regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entries made include the most important things that happen during the course of a day, especially losses, operations, important events that are of significance for the work of the unit, key briefings, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Show it on the example of the first date of war.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Metohija barracks, at 0345 hours, a wire received from the Pristina Corps with the regard to a declaration of an imminent threat of war by the federal government. So what do I do? I call in all my officers, the commanders of all the units. For example, the commanding officer of the company, the communications company, should adjust it to the situation of war. Then I order that communications should be moved to a mobile centre. Then further on, as for the Chief of Staff who commands the staff, I tell him that a mobile team should be prepared for repairing vehicles, then also reconnoitering positions, then also food for the coming period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should direct the witness to those areas of the diary that are relevant to the case. We're not interested in general information in the diary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is specific information that has to do with his brigade. I asked the witness a few moments ago what kind of entries are made, and he said of all important events, information about what they do, how orders are issued, who receives orders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a very important event at 2000 hours. There was an airstrike on the ground in Djakovica, and the operations duty officer of the MUP told me about that. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's an important event. And then the activities that I ordered, that is to say to relocate units from the locations where they had been until then. We can go on. The 26th, at the Devet Jugovica barracks aeroplanes hit the ammunition depot. Then a small group of aircraft hit the Morina barracks. Then several cruising missiles launched from the Adriatic into the interior. Then a cruising missile was shot down in the area of Zuba. Then there are several individual aircraft, one of which fired at the Devet Jugovica barracks. Then the first losses in the brigade. This was on the 31st of March when Cimbaljevic Djordje and another soldier were killed. The 31st of March, 1999, eight days into the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he describes when it happened, how they got killed. And it says, inter alia, that Lieutenant Colonel Drago Milic distinguished himself in trying to save these soldiers. The radar was totally destroyed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that you have the fifth day of war, everything recorded minute to minute?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When each aircraft came, different groups of aircraft, several crews missiles. Then all of that is at 0305, 0515, 0735, 1642, 43, 1745. 2125, 2116, 2155, 2201 hours, et cetera, et cetera, all of it in terms of hours and minutes about the airstrikes. So that is everything that is recorded in a war diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm lost on that last. I'm afraid I couldn't find it. I don't know what the accused was reading from. Perhaps I'm just not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I read out just now was the 28th of March, the fifth day of the war, where you can see the hours and minutes of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it out to you in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no need for you to read this out in detail. Is there anything else that is characteristic of this diary that you should like to draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it contains this kind of detail, details that are important for the unit, losses, activities, enemy activities, attacks by terrorists, casualties among our soldiers who were killed by Siptar terrorists. So incidents involving loss of life, woundings, major losses of resources, things that are not part of everyday activities. And in addition to that, we sent regular daily reports to the superior command, because according to a certain pattern, we reported on the situation in the unit, and this to a large extent coincides with the war diary itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you show me an example here of recording an engagement with terrorists during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this period I'd have to look it up, if you give me some time. For example, during the break I can tell you when the terrorists exactly attacked one of our units that was stationed in Rezina. Right now I'd have to look through all of this, because there are several excerpts from the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you made a statement to the Commission for Cooperation with this institution on the 28th of December, 2002. What does this statement pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with the activities of the unit on the 24th of March, that is to say precisely the day the war started. This is my own statement. And for the most part what was asked from me is to speak about what happened in the Catholic street in Djakovica, and it is below Cabrat. And I wrote about that, and I think I referred to that yesterday, too, what happened, or, rather, what we observed at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talk about what happened in Catholic street, how it was hit, and the mosque, too, and other destruction in town.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not a single gasoline station remained intact in Djakovica. And then there are secondary effects, that is to say that military facilities and other economic facilities were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Vlatko Odak also gave a statement in December. He was your subordinate; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of a battalion, and he was in charge of logistics. At the beginning of the aggression, we had to get all our equipment, all our material resources out of the Devet Jugovica barracks and that was the first one that was hit. Those days that is what he was doing. That is the task of the Logistics Battalion anyway. So he stated, I have his statement here, what he saw, what he experienced. If you wish, I can read it out, but it's all here.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need. For example, I'm just going to read out a particular quote. I hope he said this objectively. He says: "I cannot claim that NATO targeted Hadum mosque on purpose. Perhaps it had to do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the pilot's imprecision." So he looked at all of that, and he did not want to go that far, to say that they intentionally bombed the mosque and civilian targets. He said that it was perhaps imprecision, the result of inaccuracy, that that was the cause of this destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it tab 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tab 8. The last but one paragraph. That is where the quotation is that I read out a few moments ago. "I cannot claim that NATO deliberately targeted the Hadum mosque and other civilian structures. Maybe it was the result of inaccuracy or carelessness on the part of the pilots." May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, 1999, you made an order concerning measures in the event of a bombing, and you are saying that the territory of the FRY should not be violated and that we should prevent that. Is that number 9?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wrote. And this is an order of the Pristina Corps, which was adapted to my own unit, of course. So the first thing is to prevent a breakthrough by NATO forces on the attack axes and prevent a violation of the territorial integrity of the FRY, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not going to quote everything, but it also says that what should be prevented is linking up the Siptar forces with NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you referred to before. And then number 4 says: "Preventing terrorist and sabotage operations against commands and units."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4 says: "After the initial attacks, commanders command priorities will be the care of casualties, preventing panic, desertion, and criminal activities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You said preventing panic, desertion, and you haven't read the whole thing out. It also says "and criminal activities"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And criminal activities. Preventing individuals or groups from sowing discord in the unit by subversive behaviour, especially rumours about disobedience, preventing terrorist and sabotage operations against detecting and pre-empting espionage activities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a moment, please. On the 27th of December, 2002, you gave a statement to the Commission for Cooperation which pertains to the activities of your unit on the 1st of April and that has to do with the alleged crimes in Qerim?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It was given in writing. It was translated. Is this your statement, and is it in accordance with what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I wrote the statement to the commission on the basis of their request and on the basis of the alleged crime in Qerim. I explained that, I wrote this, and I signed this. And I mentioned the persons who can confirm this and who were there. And at that time I was 500 metres away from Qerim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you have the commander of the 3rd Division, Dusko Vukasinovic, who was right there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that just now. His statement -- or, rather, this is the commander of your artillery battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd Artillery Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the document that is in tab 11?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In tab 11A is a statement given by Vlatko Odak, who you also mentioned. He says that the road to Ljug Bunar leads through Qerim neighbourhood, was completely empty, that it was dark, and that they hadn't met anybody.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed the same way on that occasion, and I can confirm that it was completely dark. The road was passable. You couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In tab 12 we have your order dated 2nd of April, 1999. What does it refer to, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the application of the international law of war. I ordered that all units and all members of units must carry with them the so-called reminder for members of the army of Yugoslavia. This is my copy, and all members of the unit had to carry it with them. I also said that any persons violating the provisions of international law of war shall be reported and shall be subjected to appropriate measures, whereas the military police chief will immediately prosecute such people and turn them over to the closest military court. I also wrote: "Inform all brigade members of this order." And persons responsible for its execution were my Chief of Staff, my assistants, and unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In tab 13 we see another order of yours. What does it contain?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It describes the status of the brigade in that period. I explained yesterday how and where the brigade was deployed until the 9th of April and prior to that date. The date here is the 6th of April, and the order shows where each unit was. It says the 1st Company of the 1st Artillery Battalion is in Skivjani. The 2nd Battery of the 1st Artillery Battalion in Cabrak --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have to explain that here. Does that mean that every time when any of your units changes location an appropriate order has to be issued?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. No movement of units except in the -- in a limited area can be performed without my approval. Similarly, I had to seek approval from my corps commander to change my location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks about the taking up of positions in new areas in the next document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I issued my artillery battalion commanders appropriate orders to change location. This particular order was to the commander of the 3rd Artillery Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. What happened on the 9th of April in the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of April there was an attack, the attack, on Kosare. On that occasion Siptar terrorists supported by artillery from Albania attacked our border units in the area of Kosare killing some of my soldiers who were part of a combat group of the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the NATO Air Force active at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO aviation followed the whole thing, and I showed yesterday how the intensity of their actions, NATO action, coincided with some critical moments such as terrorists attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us a little more detail about that. What do you mean when you say the NATO followed the whole thing, the NATO aviation followed the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I showed you yesterday, and I can show it again, that strikes by NATO aviation, especially an A10 plane, an assault plane that was specifically designed to support units, this plane was most active in the area of Kosare and in the border area. It acted from our side against our forces, that is, from the territory of our country practically into the back of our units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did the planes drop any bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both bombs and rockets and cannon-balls, depending on what a particular plane was carrying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned this in your book, in tab 2 that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I describe it in my book because on that occasion one of my soldiers was killed, one officer was wounded, and another soldier got killed as well. I described it in my book, and I can read passages if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will draw your attention to one passage only, and if you think you need to add anything you will be free to do so. On page 149 of your book, and I will quote, it says: "The attack on Kosare from the territory of Albania was getting fiercer and fiercer. The enemy was relying on artillery support of the Albanian army and the fire support of NATO aviation."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Our fighters at Kosare were simply in a vice on the top of Prokletije mountains. From Albania, from the area of Bajram Curiju, the Albanian artillery was firing, and from the back, from the territory of Metohija, from the air, the NATO aviation was acting against them. Their most prominent plane in these attacks was the famous A10." On page 186, as long as we are on this tab, you say somewhere halfway down: "The first attack of NATO aviation against a column of Siptar refugees happened in the neighbourhood of Meja on the 14th of April, 1999 around 1400 hours. It was a whole massacre with a pile of burning rubble. It was not far from our position in the area of Cabrat."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "'Check what it's about. Send a team to give first aid to the casualties and report to me in detail,' said my corps commander."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My corps commander ordered me to go to the spot, to the scene to see if any assistance is necessary or can be sent and to report to him. I went there and I reported. I described it in detail in this book. Unfortunately, we didn't have a camera to make a film of it. My unit in Djakovica did not have such equipment, but soon after my arrival some cameramen arrived, and I believe there is video footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you personally left the scene immediately?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left while smoke was still coming from the corpses and the craters that were left by rockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about another order of the 10th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please have a tab number before we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is tab 15. It's a brief order, and as far as I can see, it has even been translated.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you ordered that all perpetrators of criminal offences should be immediately brought to a competent investigating judge of the Pristina Corps command military court accompanied by a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also said that unit commanders were responsible to me for the execution of this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this measure applies to volunteers and conscripts equally.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I said "volunteers-conscripts." Volunteers had the same status in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then you say: "Unit commanders are responsible to me for the execution of this order." So this is your order of the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And what is the contents of this order devoted to the protection of unit combat deployment in tab 16? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance of this order is that unit commanders must take all necessary measures to protect units, be it on the march --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do not read from it. Just read paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Any women, children, the elderly, and others encountered in the unit combat deployment sector should be -- shall be treated humanely and in line with the principles of the provisions of the international law of war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General Lazarevic also brought some orders addressed to you on the 10th of April, 1999. That is tab 17. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a very long order that details all the assessments of possible engagement with ground NATO forces. We won't go into it. On page 2, paragraph 6, he says: "Improve combat discipline and the soldierly appearance of Pristina Corps members and prevent misconduct by individuals, looting, murder, et cetera, whilst upholding the reputation of the army through your own conduct." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He also orders implementation of anti-aircraft defence measures. That applies to all units, especially my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You issued an order in tab 19. It relates to the maintenance of combat morale.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my order dated 13th April. It relates to the maintaining and strengthening of combat morale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 5 it says: "In the event of an attack by Siptar terrorist forces, they are to be crushed and destroyed quickly and efficiently."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It goes on to say: Serbian Montenegrin population and citizens of non-Serb nationality who are loyal to our country must be treated correctly and humanely." And again, my subordinate commanders are responsible to me for the implementation of that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In tab 20 we see a regular combat report. Is this the usual foremast your combat reports. Point 1, the enemy; point 2, our own forces; point 3, logistical support. To whom did you submit such reports?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always to the commander of the Pristina Corps. The form is exactly prescribed. First you cover the enemy, your own forces, then logistical support indicating expenditure of ammunition, expenditure of mines and explosives. Then you make requests, if any, or proposals. You detail the situation on the road. It was our duty to report to superior commands which roads are usable, which roads are passable, and which can be used for supply of ammunition and other resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 21 we see a criminal report dated 17th April, 1999 against some soldiers. It was submitted to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seems to be a 21 untranslated and a 21.2. Which one is it? In fact, there's several in 21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to 21, and there are several documents within this tab.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, this is the complete accompanying documentation that is regularly compiled for every criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21 is a criminal report, then follow accompanying documents, 21.1, 21.2, up to 10. This is the accompanying documentation. We won't go through it all. The substance is a criminal report for the criminal act of rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we be clear about what documents we have? I've got nothing in the section that says 21, and then I have an untranslated document in 21.1, and then I seem to have translated documents after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a full set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us just look at the titles of these documents and then we'll be able to identify which of them remain untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The index says 21 is a criminal report which is not translated yet. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly tell us, we see criminal reports here, Official Notes, statements of the accused and so on. Let me just draw your attention to these medical examinations. They are at the end of this tab. It says on the document 21.10 -- we're not going to read the name of the alleged injured party. It says: "Examination performed at 1700 hours on the 17th of April, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two doctors, two specialists signed this. As far as I can see both are --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Afrim Muhaxhiri, medical doctor, gynaecologist and ultrasound specialist. And another doctor, Hasan Manxhuka, a gynaecologist. We're not going to read the name of the victim, but they performed a detailed examination and they established that this victim that was allegedly raped was a virgin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have complete documentation concerning this case. These soldiers were from my unit, from the 3rd Artillery Battalion. And these soldiers suffered before that in an attack in Batusa. They survived this attack unlike some others. Everything is described in great detail here. They were immediately turned over to the military court in Pristina. I don't know where they were convicted, but it was up to the judicial courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't tell us what happened in this case, whether there was a conviction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot, because one of them lives on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. We can see that here. And I devoted my time more to the victims of war rather than the perpetrators of this. I am very sorry that that happened in my unit, but I didn't consider that it was up to me to investigate. I was very, very strict towards any such cases and perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps they were innocent. You're not interested in discovering that men whom you trusted as part of your command may have been wrongly accused and were in fact honourable men who were not criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until then they were indeed honourable men and were not criminals, but the moment that a criminal report was taken it is up to the courts, and I have no reason to doubt the judicial organs. I believe the courts and the decision they make, the ruling they make, will be the one that prevails.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what are the contents of your order dated the 17th of April and is to be found in tab 23? I see that it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be 22 or 23, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is providing security for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted you to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote my order, and I can read it out. I think that each of the points contained here are important. It says: "Pursuant to the order of the corps command, and in order to prevent or reduce losses among the civilian population caused by the aggressor, I hereby order: "1. That all units in the zone of responsibility of the Djakovica garrison shall take necessary measures to ensure the welfare of the civilian population. To that end, act in coordination with the MUP forces and the Djakovica Municipal Staff in order to promptly inform the civilian population of attacks by the NATO aggressors and the Siptar terrorist forces; provide necessary assistance in sheltering and evacuation; ensure optimal conditions for the relocation and accommodation for civilian population; provide assistance in delivering supplies, organising economic activities and health care; ensure full law and order and security of people and their property; prevent any infringement of the freedom and rights of citizens, unless they threaten the security of the units. "2. Where possible, select representatives or commissioners in the garrison's zone of responsibility to facilitate the more effective organisation and welfare of the population. "3. Work with the local government organs to make a thorough assessment of the size of the civilian population to facilitate the provision of supplies." At that time supplies was the number one problem in Metohija and especially in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the population of Djakovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 25.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of that number 90-something percent were Albanians, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more than 90 per cent. About 93 per cent, in fact. "4. To be responsible -- treat the civilian population extremely humanely and responsibly and in keeping with the regulations of the Yugoslav army, the international law of war and international humanitarian law. Units commanders in the Djakovica zone of responsibility shall be responsible to me for the implementation of this order. I shall personally take the strictest action to bring to account anybody who disobeys this order." It was sent out to all the units based on Djakovica territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You issued that order on the 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You also compiled a report which is to be found in tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a brief report which relates to undertaking measures against perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These three men, the perpetrators were first of all arrested, sent to a military court, and then afterwards informed their superior command. So that is the order of events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say taking the perpetrators into custody, handing them over to the competent authorities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And that is what tab 25 applies to as well. Why did you have to repeat your explanations in greater detail. You informed the corps command in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was customary. That is to say if an event took place, a crime took place in one unit, the corps command sent a circular piece of information to other units to inform them as a preventive measure and as a warning and caution that nothing like that should be repeated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that -- those are the contents of tab 25. Tab 26, as far as I can see, is once again your order, the command of the 52nd Brigade of the PVO. I'm not going to dwell on that now. Could you just read out point 4 of the order. And the end of point 6.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As concerns relations with the civilian population, adhere to the previous orders in every way. Use all means available to comprehensively prevent any threats to the safety of civilians and their property."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you said: "And completely prevent or comprehensively prevent."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here. Yes, "comprehensively prevent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as concerns relations with the civilian population, adhere to the previous orders in every way, use all means available to comprehensively prevent any threats to the safety of civilians and their property."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now as far as point 6 is concerned. Point 6, please, just the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about volunteers here who were in the unit as recruits, volunteers who cannot carry out the tasks or any kind of legal action, to return if they cannot carry out their assignments. But it says: "Persons responsible for crimes and other actions shall be handed over to the brigade command NOB so that their responsibility may be established and further steps taken." And may I comment on that. I'd like to say that because they were volunteers who reported people came -- they were 50 year olds sometimes. They'd come to the unit. They can't see very well, can't hear very well, and they're not really very useful to us, so we sent those back. We sent them back from the unit so as not to be ballast and a burden to us. But we checked everybody out before sending them back. We checked whether they had taken part in any criminal acts or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. Then point 7. What does point 7 mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The team tasked in my last order with clearing up the terrain shall continue to carry out clearing up the terrain across the brigade's deployment area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this asanacija, clearing up of the terrain mean and imply?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant dealing with animal remains, human remains, any noxious matter or anything else that is detrimental to the human environment and can lead to contamination and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, I wasn't clear about your reference to volunteers there. I understood you earlier to say that you did have a certain number of volunteers. You gave us a number who came from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Republika Srpska, I think, and then you mentioned anyone else who was added at the time would be a reservist. Is this now a third category of volunteer that existed? Who were these people, then, referred to in this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you heard me properly. First of all, I said from Republika Srpska there was just one volunteer. Her name was Dragojanka and she was a nurse. That's the first point. Secondly, all the volunteers that came to us from the unit were from Serbia. Then military conscripts but were not members of the anti-aircraft defence unit. And amongst them -- anti-defence unit. And amongst them they were elderly persons, infirmed persons sometimes. They came to the unit, whereas they weren't actually able physically to meet the demands that a unit would have. So we would send that kind of person back or send them on to another unit where some use was found for them. Our unit was manned by young people because air defence required young people, people who can act quickly, manoeuvre quickly, who can see properly, hear properly, and so on. And they had to be fast in order to able to escape the onslaughts of the airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean that paragraph 6 in this order refers to the 80 or so volunteers you mentioned earlier that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does refer to those from the Pristina command. They were brought in with all the documents and handed over to the unit and deployed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, in the first paragraph of the same document, which is tab 26, you -- the document we are looking at right now, tab 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You expressed your concerns as the reason why you are giving this order. Among them is an interesting passage. In the middle of the first paragraph you said you're concerned about the physical appearance, particularly of the reserve forces, is not consistent with the norm, which is damaging to the reputation of the Yugoslav army. Also, there have been instances of criminal activities by individuals which has had an exceptionally negative impact on the overall security situation. So if you could give me some more examples of physical appearances which is damaging the reputation of VJ. What do you mean? What did you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I meant by it is this: People who were getting on in years, who had been issued equipment as soldiers after they left their -- the army, the uniforms were no longer the right size, some of them were dirty and old. They might have spent several days in one position during the war, and it was difficult to replace their equipment, their uniforms, to keep them clean and tidy, and others whose uniforms didn't fit them. So when these people turned up, and as I said they did come to Djakovica while they were still able to call their families and contact their families, they presented quite a different appearance than the soldiers. The soldiers were the ones who wore new uniforms. They fitted them better. They looked better in their uniforms. They were younger and so on. So they struck a better appearance. Just like myself. I'm sure that a uniform suited me much better which was younger than it does now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I take it from this statement that there might have been some volunteers who wore special insignia which was different from the normal one or who carried some knives? Do you exclude such possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had there been people like that it would have been set out in the preamble. If you look at this preamble, the description there relates to any acts that might take place or might have taken place in some other unit. And I explained a moment ago that information about rape, for example, a rape, an instance of rape that took place in my unit was sent out to other units, a circular piece of information as a warning and caution to prevent such things from happening in their area of responsibility. So it was sent out to the continue corps. And there were no other uniforms and the uniforms worn by the Yugoslav army and police. Uniforms might be better, not so good, older, newer, faded uniforms, even torn uniforms. But all the uniforms were of the same type, the same type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only example you've given in response to Judge Kwon's question relates to uniforms. Is it not strange that that's not actually mentioned? It's physical appearance of the reserve forces. It's not the state of the uniforms of the reserve forces that's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personal appearance depends on one's natural appearance, one's clothing, one's haircut. There were those who hadn't had a haircut, who were untidy. And given the circumstances in which they lived and worked, there were of course people who weren't tidy. There were those who had dirty boots, if they happened to come in from such area which was muddy, for example. So all that goes to make up one's personal appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a bit of confusion in terms of what personal appearance implies, General. So can you just tell us the following: For example, when a soldier does not wear a cap, does that mean infringing upon personal appearance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if is unshaven?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any kind of untidiness in terms of the uniform they wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does all of that belong to personal appearance? You also described other things like dirty boots or dirty or unkempt clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even when a button is not buttoned. That is not considered to be proper from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 you spoke about clearing up the terrain and you explained what you meant by it, asanacija. Now, in relation to that, there is a document in tab 27. Since you explained that this clearing up the terrain means removing everything that may be hazardous to health or in any other way harm the population, what have you got here in tab 27? You sent this urgently to the Pristina Corps command, a report.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is report that my chief of ABHO submitted and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us exactly what it means, chief of ABHO. Perhaps they don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an excerpt for nuclear, biological, chemical weapons. Everything that can harm the health of human beings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does it say here? In the area of Osek Hilja, three kilometres north of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cellar of a house a certain quantity of flour was found, about ten tonnes. The flour had been delivered to the inhabitants belonging to the Siptar ethnic minority as part of a humanitarian aid shipment by the Mother Teresa humanitarian organisation. The flour was contaminated using a DR M-3 radiation detector and found to be radioactively contaminated 1 to 3 Microgrey per hour. It was later established that three tonnes had been issued to a bakery to make bread. Steps were taken to stop the production of the bread and the flour was withdrawn from circulation. "The flour is being withdrawn and a pit is being dug at the town rubbish bump to bury the flour. The pit will be visibly marked."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does all of that fall been the purview of this clearing up of the terrain, taking care of the health of the population, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the brigade, I had a chief of ABHO who controlled every activity, and after every explosion after bomb or a rocket he went to see whether there was higher radiation or not, and that is where -- that is how we found out that there was more radiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that as for your statement in tab 28 and tab 29 is something that has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that is the case because we dwelled on that when looking at those statements of Nik Peraj. So then I refer to these exhibits, and I hope they were admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They have already been admitted. They have already been admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same subject, your comrades in arms, Vlatko Odak, Vlatko Vukovic, Vukadinovic, and Rakovic gave statements. They are in tab 30. 30, 30A, 30B. All of these statements pertain to --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit that was adjacent to my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. These statements of theirs, do they correspond with your own testimony here in relation to these events that they describe and that you already spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not an acceptable method of getting evidence in. I'm going to, of course, object to these statements for other reasons. Either there's something in them that the accused wishes to draw to our attention or they shouldn't really be admitted. If he's simply saying that these statements are identical with his own account, I suppose the question arises why but in one way or another pretty unsatisfactory in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you be seeking to have these statements admitted, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think they should be admitted. They have to do with the same event that General Djosan testified about. These are his comrades in arms. They spoke of the same matter that has to do with Meja and Korenica. And the witness already testified about that, showed the map, et cetera. If I'm supposed to go through each and every one of them I can do it, but I thought that they could be identified, that he knew about the statements, that he read them. This is in his exhibits. They're authentic, and there's no discrepancy between what they say and what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The procedure for admission of this kind of evidence would be Rule 92 bis, quite plainly, as they're statements by another party who could be a witness, and they're cumulative of this testimony. Mr. Milosevic has here Mr. Tomanovic at the moment. It would be quite simple to put in a covering filing and serve the matter on the Prosecution in that way. It can be admissible but it depends how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Kay, was whether in the evidence of General Delic anything of a similar nature was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Statements given to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I couldn't remember. There may be. I may be wrong, but my -- my recollection is no. I don't know whether Mr. Nice has a recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that, as I said earlier today, I think, or yesterday, that the statements have not been admitted. Indeed, there's been a very major exercise being undertaken to deal with exhibits marked for identification, and that's enabled us to focus on one or two exhibits that may be problematic, and I think the position is that the small recently produced maps have been admitted, I'm not quite sure on what basis, but that the statements have not been admitted, other than the statements by any witness himself, Delic, and now this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I assist? I think Odak is going to be a witness fairly soon, so that deals with this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have not admitted statements like this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the maps, I think as a way of presentation of testimony they're very useful, and I can't see any objection to that as an aid. Plenty of examples in the Prosecution case where we had schematic diagrams put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're going to call this -- if you're going to call the maker of this statement, Colonel Odak, then you might as well wait for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I wonder why he needs to call Odak again when we have this general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll deal with the admissibility of this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement shortly. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to these statements, have you read Odak's, Vukovic's, Vukadinovic's, and Ratkovic's statements?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness's microphone is off. We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any contradictions in terms of what they stated in relation to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just go into greater detail because they were on site but there is no discrepancy. After all, I could not have written a statement that would have been contrary to the knowledge of my immediate subordinates there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 30th of April, you compiled a regular combat report, and it is contained in tab 31. Is this a regular combat report, the kind that is regularly submitted, or does it have something special that you would like to indicate?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is regular combat report, the kind we sent in every day. Here I inform the corps command that I decided to transfer part of my units, and I'm notifying them that reconnaissance will be carried out in terms of the new command post. As always, we talk about the ammunition spent, the weapons used, et cetera. So it doesn't really differ from other such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the documents is the information you sent on the 3rd of May, 1999, and it has to do with the -- or, rather, this is tab 32. What is this about very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event in Skivjani, or rather, in Osek Hilja, where there was an attempted rape, a soldier, attempted rape, and I took certain measures. Here it is stated exactly what kind of action was taken against the man who attempted rape. He was handed over to a military court. His commanding officer was punished and so on. Those are the measures that I took as commander. As soon as he was handed over to the military court, then regular procedure follows, a criminal report, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muharem Ibraj gentleman testified about this event here except that he did not have this information, but it matches.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire brigade was informed about all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You compiled a report on the 4th of May. It has to do with the civilian population, as far as I can see. What is the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is actually a report to the command of the Pristina Corps, and we informed them about measures to protect the civilian population. It says: "Based on the above-mentioned order, we hereby inform you that the civilian population has been accommodated in the following sectors: "The villages of Peskote, Osek Hilja, et cetera, where the civilian population is, then the town of Djakovica has a population of 35.000 to 40.000, and there are another 20.000 to 25.000 inhabitants in villages. And that the possible reception areas for newly displaced persons are in the Bistrazin village sector since the NATO airstrikes were still on."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say also in conclusion that you have taken all other measures mentioned in your order concerning the protection of the civilian population. That is a quotation from the end.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have another regular command -- combat report in tab 34. It also talks about the enemy, our forces. Is there anything characteristic here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Cabrat is targeted here. I said that we reported about everything that affected our unit, and this deals with it chronologically. At 1840, two rocket projectiles. At 1852 hours, again two rocket projectiles. This corroborates the map that I explained yesterday. Then further on we inform the command that we also fired at the air force but that there were no effects. In this way, we justified the materiel resources used or, rather, the materiel used. I say we fire at aircraft and that we used 1.240 bullets but that there was no effect. Our obligation was to give reports on materiel all the time because of the fact that it was very hard to provide adequate supplies to units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what does the document in tab 35 pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this document, and it also has to do with improving the appearance of soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia, specifically our units. It would happen that when soldiers went on furlough they would go into restaurants and coffee bars with -- wearing uniforms, with weapons in their hands, and in this way they behaved improperly. That is why my order was to prohibit their entry into hotels, high-class hotels where foreign guests were staying, diplomats, et cetera, so that there would not be extra pressure in this way. Again, my order states that the commander is in charge of having it seen through, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab -- tab 36. It only relates to communication through letters.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's very important to say this: Since we had a lot of soldiers and reservists who destroyed the repeater -- with the destruction of the repeater, rather, and damage to the television building and other damage remained totally cut off from their families. I instructed that they should write letters to be delivered to their parents to ensure continued communication, because sometimes parents would come to Djakovica having no clue where their children were. So this was to ensure communication and to reassure the parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab -- let me see. Tab 37 contains an order, your order that pertains to certain measures. Which measures? Would you please explain it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ensuring work order and discipline. I issued this order, as I have always insisted, that every measure possible be used to maintain an adequate order of -- level of order and discipline, to prevent criminal offences and violations, to maintain work and discipline at a maximum level, as well as to prevent self-willed use of motor vehicles outside of combat disposition but also within the framework of combat disposition. Everybody was able to drive vehicles but only as prescribed by the combat disposition of their unit. Prevent and completely eradicate unauthorised use of motor vehicles. That's number 3. And then make maximum use of the Military Police Platoon to establish order, check general security and maintain traffic security on roads, particularly on approaches to Djakovica, in the town and villages. This was submitted to all the unit commanders and they were responsible for execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In number 38 we say an order from General Lazarevic that you received. It says here subordinate commanding officer, brigade commander. What does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the fact that there was increased incidence of attacks by Siptar terrorists groups against columns of the army of Yugoslavia, and units frequently suffered losses during such attacks. Mines were laid on the road in most cases and resulting losses were heavy. I saw with my own eyes how mines were laid inside the asphalt so that it was practically indiscernible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 39, there's some sort of warning also sent by General Lazarevic. What does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from the previous order and warns against the most dangerous roads, access roads to Metohija mainly, that were used as supply route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Follows a report on security and political situation that we will not dwell upon, but there is also a list of casualties from bombing compiled by Dr. Stanojevic, specialist of radiology. What kind of list is this? How did these people die?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of names of people who were the victims of the previous day's bombing in Meja, and whenever we were able to identify the corpses that were not completely incinerated, we listed their names. The victims were placed in the Djakovica hospital, and we see the names of 43 people that were identified, people who were killed in Meja. They all come from surrounding populated areas, Fsaj, Molic, Sismon, Racaj, Glodjan, et cetera. It's mainly women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You complain about time, but I observe that you have gone past the estimated time, your estimated time. In that regard -- let me -- in that regard, I have to say that we will have the Status Conference tomorrow morning, in the first half of tomorrow morning. That's the Status Conference relating to the use of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you hold in your hands this report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic did not give a tab number. We have no reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What tab is that? 41. 41.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 41. No, I did not exhibit this here. It's your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the general is this final report submitted to the prosecutor to be reviewed concerning the NATO campaign against Yugoslavia? Do you have this report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to tell us as a specialist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what number is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not include it in my exhibits. It's your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How can we find it, by what reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm completely mystified. I think the accused is suggesting that this is a document that's been produced by the Prosecution. If he or the witness, who has obviously come prepared for this, if he hands that document I might be able to establish whether we can find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. This is a document titled -- it's an official document of your institution. It's called "Final report submitted to the Prosecutor by a commission set up to review the campaign, the bombing campaign, by NATO against Yugoslavia." It explains various actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a document of the court or those prosecuting this case at this moment. If the accused wants such a document to be available, it's simply got to make it available in the usual way for us to look at. They don't sit here on shelves waiting to be pulled out, and I don't know where I can find this document rapidly now. And we certainly can't deal with it with the accused leafing through it and decide what line to look at at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope the witness can put it on the overhead projector and just give us his professional observations regarding what is written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it in English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must say it's beginning to sound a bit as though we're reaching that habitual terminal flourish where a general opinion is required from a witness on some issue or other that may or may not be of interest or relevance. I'm a bit cautious about this, and I would invite the Chamber to be similarly. If this is a document that emanated from the Prosecution dealing with the possibility of NATO being pursued by this court, then any opinion on it from this witness is unlikely to be of any value whatsoever. But we have to know what the document is first. We can't deal with it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we're dealing with the report by Madam Del Ponte in relation to investigation of NATO war crimes in the bombing of Yugoslavia. That's the document we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say you're going to make of this document, Mr. Milosevic? There's a suspicion that it might be non-forensic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what kind of suspicion there is, but I wanted to hear the opinion of General Djosan, because his speciality is in air defence and the activities mentioned here. NATO action was precisely from the air, so I wanted to hear what he thinks about the claims in this report. If you believe it's irrelevant, maybe you want to tell me that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't want to hear it because nobody seems to want to hear anything about NATO crimes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to find out first, Mr. Milosevic, what the document says. What does the document purport to do? And then I'll determine whether the witness can assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here's what it says: In the contents we see that it's about basic data, mandate, programme of work, general issues, environmental damage, use of projectiles containing deleted uranium, use of cluster bombs. These are all issues dealt with by the witness. He now even showed a map where we can see where exactly projectiles with depleted uranium were used. He spoke about the use of cluster bombs and so on. I'm not going to ask him about the legal issues involved in the choice of targets or legal regulations. There is also talk about the number of targets, number of victims, the general objectives of the campaign, specific incidents, attack on a passenger train, attack on the convoy in Djakovica where this witness was, attack on the radio television building, attack on the Chinese Embassy, Korisa village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I said we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask one question. Mr. Kay, the accused described the document as a final report submitted to the Prosecutor by a commission set up to review the bombing campaign by NATO against Yugoslavia. You understand it to be a report by the Prosecutor. Now, we need to be clear, first of all, what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the document that was in my mind that I took it to be from the references made by the accused. Maybe he could clarify that, whether it is the report by Mrs. Del Ponte containing the information from NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the official report. There is no signature here, but it was published, it says here, by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. It's the final report made by them when the idea appeared to review possible crimes by NATO and issued that covered -- that were dealt with by this witness.
